_about: Long stories that play out over weeks, told by real returning golfers. A story casts its roles ('from': 'new' makes a named regular who joins the club; 'member' borrows a member who fits) and walks a chain of stages. A stage waits for its 'when' (visit, round, hole, days, request, tournament, month; 'if' and 'now' fire at once), then posts its 'say' lines to the feed, puts a 'bubble' over a character, shows a 'toast', applies an 'effect' (mood, tip, money, members, home, celebrity, match, flag, buzz, rating_bias) and moves to 'next', or ends ('end': happy, sad or quiet). 'chapter' is the sentence the Stories panel shows while a stage waits; 'request' is what the club could do to move it on, with 'deadline' days and the 'else' stage when time runs out. Text takes {a} {b} (names), {a_first}, {course}, {hole}, {event}, {stake}.

stages.chapter: Dot Harrow and Ray Tolliver, strangers, have been put in the same group.

say.text: Got paired with a stranger who talks to his ball. He calls it Gerald.
Played with a woman who hums on the backswing. Didn't miss a putt.

stages.chapter: They keep booking the same tee time and calling it a coincidence.

say.text: Same tee time as the ball-talker. Coincidence. Definitely a coincidence.

request.text: a bench within a chip of the water

stages.chapter: After their rounds they walk down to the water and stand about awkwardly. A bench there would help.

say.text: Someone put a bench by the water. We sat on it for an hour and talked about nothing. It was great.

toast.text: Dot and Ray have found the bench by the water. Something is happening.

stages.chapter: Ray has been practising a speech. On the course, to his ball.

say.text: Asked her on the last green. She said 'you'll have to fix that slice first'. Then she said yes.

toast.text: Ray proposed to Dot on the last green, and she said yes.

stages.chapter: The wedding is booked for the clubhouse.

say.text: Married on a golf course. My mother is furious. Best day of my life.

toast.text: Dot and Ray married at the clubhouse. The party paid $1,500 for the room and three of the guests joined the club.

stages.ending: Dot and Ray married at the clubhouse. Gerald was best man.

say.text: Nice course. Nothing to sit on, though.

stages.ending: Dot and Ray drifted apart. There was nowhere to sit.

stories.title: The Grudge
stories.blurb: Two regulars who cannot stand each other.

stages.chapter: {a} and {b} disagree about handicaps, and everything else.

say.text: {b_first} says he's a 12 handicap. {b_first} is not a 12 handicap.
{a_first} counts his own putts. Loosely.

stages.chapter: {b} is waiting for a birdie to rub in.

say.text: Birdie on {hole}. {a_first}, if you're reading this, and you are: birdie.

stages.chapter: {a} has had enough. There is talk of money.

say.text: Fine. Money match. Here. Next weekend. Bring cash.

toast.text: {a} and {b} have agreed a grudge match on your course, and {a_first} wants the owner in it too, for a stake of his own.

stages.chapter: The match is on. The whole club is watching.

say.text: Lost to {b_first} AND the owner. Selling my clubs. Keeping the hat.

stages.ending: {a} lost the grudge match to {b} and the owner, and took it badly. The bar did well.

say.text: {a_first} lost. To me. I have it on video. The video is 40 minutes long and I will send it to anyone.

stages.ending: {b} won the grudge match and has a 40 minute video to prove it.

say.text: {b_first} and I have agreed to never speak of handicaps again. Starting now.

stages.ending: {a} and {b} declared a truce. Nobody believes it.

stories.title: The Comeback
stories.blurb: A tour pro who stopped, trying to start again.

stages.chapter: Hal Brennan, who once played the tour, is trying to find his swing again.

say.text: Haven't picked up a club in four years. The grip felt like shaking hands with a stranger.

stages.chapter: Hal is playing badly and blaming nobody but himself.

say.text: Shot a million. Course is fine. I'm the problem.

stages.chapter: Hal keeps coming back. That is something.

say.text: Found something on the range today. The old move. Don't tell anyone.

stages.chapter: Hal is one good hole away from believing it.

say.text: Birdie. First one since the Buick Open. I'm not crying, you're crying.

toast.text: Hal Brennan just made his first birdie in four years, on your course.

stages.chapter: Hal wants a word with the owner.

say.text: Spoke to the owner. If they'll have me, I'll teach here. Cheap. I owe this place.

toast.text: Hal Brennan has offered to be your club pro for a fraction of the usual wage. Hire a club pro from Staff and he's yours.

stages.ending: Hal Brennan found his swing here and offered to teach for next to nothing.

say.text: Gave it a go. Some things stay in the past.

stages.ending: Hal Brennan never found the birdie he needed, and went back to selling insurance.

stories.title: The View
stories.blurb: She wants a house. The house wants a view.

stages.chapter: Celestine Vaux is house-hunting and has her eye on hole {hole}. The view from it wants work.

say.text: Drove out to look at the land. The land is fine. The view from {hole} wants work.

request.text: something to look at along hole {hole} (trees, flowers, water) and a home site for sale

stages.chapter: Celestine comes back every week to look at hole {hole} and sigh.

say.text: Someone planted the view. I'll take the house. Have my people call your people. You have people?

toast.text: Celestine Vaux bought a home on hole {hole}, and two of her friends joined the club to be near her.

stages.ending: Celestine Vaux bought a house on hole {hole} once there was something to look at.

say.text: Bought in Tuscany instead. Nice talking to you.

stages.ending: Celestine Vaux bought in Tuscany. The view there was ready.

stories.title: The Prodigy
stories.blurb: Fourteen years old and already better than you.

stages.chapter: A fourteen-year-old called Jun Okafor is beating everyone on your course.

say.text: Mum dropped me off. Said be back by six. Shot two under by five.

stages.chapter: Jun is collecting birdies and missing homework.

say.text: Birdie on {hole}. Again. Teacher says I should focus on fractions. This IS fractions.

stages.chapter: Jun wants a tournament to enter. Host one (Tournaments) and the kid will be in it.

say.text: Third in the {event}. Against adults. With a borrowed putter.

toast.text: Jun Okafor, fourteen, finished third in the {event}. People are talking.

stages.chapter: Jun has gone quiet. Rumour says a sponsor called.

say.text: Signed. First purchase: a putter that isn't borrowed. Second: a round at {course}, where it started.

toast.text: Jun Okafor has turned professional and is coming back to play the course where it started. Cameras are following.

stages.ending: Jun Okafor turned pro and came home to play, with half the golf press in tow.

say.text: No tournaments here. The club down the road has one every month. Just saying.

stages.ending: Jun Okafor went looking for a tournament somewhere else.

stories.title: The Critic
stories.blurb: Two visits, one review, and a lot riding on the sandwiches.

stages.chapter: Margaret Pell of Golf Weekly is on the course under her own name, which is not how incognito works. Her next visit decides the review.

say.text: Reviewing a course today. Incognito. Please nobody read this.

stages.chapter: Margaret has one more round before she files. Everything counts.

say.text: Review's in. 'Honest, funny, unexpectedly good.' I meant the course. Mostly.

toast.text: Golf Weekly's review is glowing. The course rating gets a lift for the next three months.

stages.ending: Margaret Pell's review called the course 'unexpectedly good'. It stuck.

say.text: Review's in. I used the word 'adequate' four times. The editor cut two.

toast.text: Golf Weekly's review was lukewarm. The course rating takes a knock for two months.

stages.ending: Margaret Pell called the course 'adequate'. Twice, in print.

stories.title: The Quiet Hole
stories.blurb: A retired couple who want one hole to themselves.

stages.chapter: The Pargeters want one quiet hole: hole {hole}, with a bench on it and no cart path near it.

say.text: June and I like a quiet hole. One bench. No carts rattling past. Is that so much?

request.text: a bench beside hole {hole} and no cart path within three tiles of it

stages.chapter: The Pargeters play hole {hole} and look for somewhere to sit.

say.text: Sat on the bench on {hole} for an hour. June saw a heron. I saw June see a heron.

stages.chapter: June has been talking to Walter about the clubhouse roof.

say.text: Walter wrote the club a cheque. I let him think it was his idea.

toast.text: The Pargeters donated $2,500 to the clubhouse fund.

stages.ending: The Pargeters got their quiet hole and gave the club $2,500.

say.text: We tried. We'll be at the bowls club.

stages.ending: The Pargeters gave up on a quiet hole and took up bowls.

stories.title: Content
stories.blurb: 2.3 million followers are about to see your course.

stages.chapter: Brix Dalloway, 2.3 million followers, is filming her round. How it goes decides what she posts.

say.text: On a golf course today for CONTENT. 2.3 million of you are about to learn what a 'par' is.

stages.chapter: The cameras are rolling. Keep her fed, watered and out of the water.

say.text: Okay the golf course is actually fire? Posting the whole thing. Go.

toast.text: Brix Dalloway's video of your course is everywhere. Expect a crowd.

stages.ending: Brix Dalloway's video sent a crowd your way.

say.text: Rating this golf course: the sandwich was dry and I lost eleven balls. 2 out of 10.

toast.text: Brix Dalloway gave the course 2 out of 10 to 2.3 million people.

stages.ending: Brix Dalloway gave the course 2 out of 10. The sandwich was dry.
